title: Myelodysplastic syndromes and premalignant clonal hematopoiesis

units.name: Introduction
units.assessment: Can you define MDS in one sentence that includes clonality, ineffective hematopoiesis and cytopenias, and explain how clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential sits upstream of it on the same biological continuum?

lesson.title: Dr. Danielle Hammond: Clonal Hematopoiesis In Clinical Practice - The Good, The Bad and The Ugly
lesson.why: A full clinician-facing hour on what clonal hematopoiesis actually means in practice, which is the frame this chapter uses to introduce MDS and its precursor states.

drills.name: Which genes define CHIP and what they predict
drills.title: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP): genes, disease predisposition & potential
drills.channel: VJHemOnc – Video Journal of Hematology & HemOnc

units.name: Epidemiology
units.assessment: Can you state roughly how MDS incidence changes with age, name the acquired exposures that raise risk, and say when a young patient with MDS should trigger a search for a germline predisposition syndrome?

lesson.title: Aging and Clonal Diseases (Aging Patient: Dispelling Myths)
lesson.why: An EHA session on why clonal myeloid disease is fundamentally a disease of ageing hematopoiesis, which is the single most important epidemiological fact about MDS.

units.name: Biology
units.assessment: Can you group the recurrently mutated genes in MDS into their functional classes — spliceosome, DNA methylation, chromatin, transcription factors, signalling and TP53 — and explain mechanistically why ineffective hematopoiesis produces cytopenias despite a hypercellular marrow?

lesson.title: The Origins and Evolution of MDS - Dr. Benjamin Ebert
lesson.why: Benjamin Ebert on how MDS clones arise and evolve, tying founder mutations in ageing stem cells to the ineffective hematopoiesis that defines the disease.

units.assessment: Can you separate CHIP, CCUS, ICUS and MDS using variant allele fraction, the presence of cytopenias and marrow morphology, and say what the clonal hematopoiesis risk score adds when counselling a patient about transformation risk?

lesson.title: Pre MDS states CH, CCUS, ICUS – How to manage in the clinic?
lesson.why: Exactly this section's question — how to actually manage a patient who turns up with CHIP, CCUS or ICUS rather than how to define the terms.

units.name: Clinical presentation
units.assessment: Can you describe the typical presentation of MDS — which cytopenia dominates, why the anemia is usually macrocytic, and which autoinflammatory syndromes such as VEXAS should make you look for an underlying clonal marrow disorder?

lesson.title: MDS - Myeloplastic Syndromes - 2023 Best of Hematology Conference
lesson.why: A conference-level clinical overview that starts where patients actually present — cytopenias found on a routine count — and works forward to the marrow findings.

units.name: Diagnostic evaluation
units.assessment: Can you list what a complete MDS workup must include beyond the CBC — marrow aspirate and biopsy with iron stain, karyotype, next-generation sequencing, flow — and name the reversible mimics that must be excluded before dysplasia is called clonal?

lesson.title: Clinical Implications of Genetic Mutations in Myelodysplastic Syndromes
lesson.why: Shows how the sequencing and cytogenetic results are actually read at diagnosis, including which mutations change the diagnosis rather than merely the prognosis.

units.name: Classification
units.assessment: The WHO 5th edition and the ICC both rewrote MDS classification in 2022 — can you name the genetically defined entities each recognises (SF3B1-mutated, del(5q), biallelic TP53) and say where the two systems disagree about blast thresholds and the MDS/AML boundary?

lesson.title: A classification of myelodysplastic syndromes that aids clinical decision-making
lesson.why: A 2024 talk built specifically around the post-2022 classification and how the genetically defined categories change what you do at the bedside.

units.assessment: Can you separate the goals of therapy in lower-risk versus higher-risk MDS, say which patients are candidates for allogeneic transplant and when they should be referred, and state what determines whether an asymptomatic lower-risk patient is simply observed?
